short: Six centuries of rule over the Balkans, Anatolia and the Arab world.
full:
Osman, a frontier chieftain in Bithynia, is conventionally credited with founding the state around 1299, though the date rests on later tradition rather than contemporary record. His successors crossed into Europe in the 1350s, absorbed the Balkans, took Constantinople in 1453 and made it the capital, and under Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent added Egypt, Syria, the Hijaz, Hungary and command of the eastern Mediterranean. The sultan claimed the caliphate as well, and the empire ruled on three continents.

The failure before Vienna in 1683 began a long retreat. Nineteenth-century sultans rebuilt the army and rewrote the law codes while Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away and European creditors took charge of the debt. Defeat in the First World War brought occupation and a partition treaty that Mustafa Kemal's national movement refused to accept. The Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate on 1 November 1922, and Mehmed VI left Istanbul on a British warship.
